stem: A client who injects drugs develops severe progressive back pain, fever, leg weakness, and new urinary dysfunction. Which complication should the nurse suspect first?

options.A: Spinal epidural abscess with possible spinal cord or cauda equina compression requiring immediate evaluation.
options.B: Uncomplicated mechanical back strain because fever and progressive neurologic deficits are common findings in muscle injury.
options.C: Simple cystitis because urinary dysfunction explains the back pain and progressive leg weakness.
options.D: Chronic degenerative disk disease that can be evaluated routinely after the fever resolves.

rationale: A is correct. Current NCBI guidance identifies injection drug use as a risk factor for spinal epidural abscess. Presentations are variable, but progressive back pain, fever, and neurologic deficits are important red flags; advanced disease may cause weakness, sensory changes, bowel or bladder dysfunction, or paralysis from neural compression. MRI with contrast is the imaging modality of choice, and neurologic deterioration can become irreversible if evaluation and treatment are delayed. B, C, and D fail to explain the combined infectious and progressive neurologic syndrome.
educational_objective: Recognize progressive back pain with fever and new motor or bladder/bowel dysfunction in a high-risk client as possible spinal epidural abscess requiring immediate MRI-based evaluation and urgent multidisciplinary management.
source_organization: National Library of Medicine / NCBI StatPearls
source_version_date: Spinal Epidural Abscess last updated November 8, 2025; Epidural Abscess last updated April 12, 2026; accessed 2026-08-17
source_locator: Spinal Epidural Abscess — History and Physical: classic triad is uncommon; red flags include fever, neurologic deficits and active infection; risk factors include intravenous drug use. Progressive disease can cause weakness, saddle/perianal sensory loss, urinary or bowel dysfunction, and paralysis. Evaluation: contrast-enhanced MRI is the imaging modality of choice. Epidural Abscess — Treatment/Management and Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes: SEA can progress rapidly to irreversible neurologic deficits and requires immediate diagnosis and intervention.
source_claim_supported: Injection drug use increases SEA risk; progressive back pain with fever and new neurologic or bladder/bowel deficits requires urgent evaluation for spinal epidural abscess, with MRI as preferred imaging and prompt intervention needed to limit irreversible injury.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing
blueprint_locator: Physiological Integrity — Physiological Adaptation: recognize signs and symptoms of acute neurologic complications and intervene; identify rapid deterioration requiring emergency escalation.
blueprint_topic: Physiological Adaptation — spinal epidural abscess and cord-compression recognition
correction_summary: Rebuilt the source item to include high-value neurologic red flags and removed the implication that the classic back-pain/fever/deficit triad is always present. The final item tests urgent recognition and imaging rather than memorization of a symptom list.
audit_reviewer: OpenAI GPT-5.6 Sol — Rule 1 clinical audit + adversarial second pass

audit_findings.clinical_category: spinal epidural abscess/spinal cord compression/infectious neurologic emergency
audit_findings.source_audit: Verified against NCBI Spinal Epidural Abscess updated November 2025 and Epidural Abscess updated April 2026.
audit_findings.claim_by_claim: A integrates risk factor, infection, progressive pain and neurologic/bladder deficits. B-D cannot account for the full syndrome and would cause unsafe delay.
audit_findings.choice_A: Correct; suspected SEA with neural compression requires immediate evaluation.
audit_findings.choice_B: Incorrect; mechanical strain does not explain fever plus progressive neurologic dysfunction.
audit_findings.choice_C: Incorrect; cystitis does not explain progressive leg weakness in this context.
audit_findings.choice_D: Incorrect; routine delay is unsafe with neurologic progression.
audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Vertebral osteomyelitis/discitis can coexist or mimic SEA, but the neurologic compression signs make SEA the highest-priority complication to exclude. Only A provides the appropriate emergency response.
audit_findings.cueing: All options interpret the same back-pain/infection/neurologic presentation.
audit_findings.blueprint: Rapid neurologic-complication recognition fits Physiological Adaptation.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: Rechecked the low sensitivity of the classic triad, MRI role, injection-drug-use risk, vertebral osteomyelitis overlap, and bladder/bowel red flags. No unsupported numeric thresholds or second answer remained.
